metadata.title: Cocktail Crossword
metadata.description: The definitive mixology crossword game combining craft recipes, distillation lore, bar history, and wordcraft.

codex.name: Negroni
codex.method: Stirred over ice until chilled and diluted (~30s)
codex.garnish: Expressed orange peel swath or fresh wheel
codex.formula:
1.0 oz (30 ml) London Dry Gin
1.0 oz (30 ml) Campari
1.0 oz (30 ml) Sweet Vermouth
codex.tip: Equal parts simplicity hides a delicate thermal balance. Stir for 30–40 seconds to achieve 25% dilution, which opens botanical aromatics and softens bitter gentian.
codex.lore: Legend holds that Count Camillo Negroni asked bartender Fosco Scarselli at Caffè Casoni in Florence to strengthen his favorite Americano by swapping soda water for gin.

codex.name: Sazerac
codex.subline: Official Cocktail of New Orleans c. 1850s
codex.method: Stirred with ice, strained into absinthe-rinsed glass
codex.ice: Ice in mixing glass only; none in service glass
codex.garnish: Expressed lemon twist (expressed over top and discarded)
codex.formula:
2.0 oz (60 ml) Rye Whiskey (or Cognac)
0.25 oz (7.5 ml) Rich Demerara Syrup (or 1 sugar cube)
3–4 dashes Peychaud's Bitters
1 dash Angostura Bitters
Absinthe wash/rinse
codex.tip: Pack the serving rocks glass with crushed ice to freeze the crystal while you stir the cocktail. Dump the ice, coat the cold glass interior with an absinthe atomizer or rinse, then strain.
codex.lore: Originally crafted with Sazerac de Forge et Fils Cognac at the Sazerac Coffee House. When phylloxera devastated French vineyards in the 1870s, local bartenders transitioned to Maryland and Pennsylvania rye whiskeys.

codex.name: The Sour Family
codex.subline: The Cornerstone of Balance (Spirit, Citrus, Sugar)
codex.method: Vigorously shaken with ice (optional dry shake for egg white)
codex.ice: Strained neat into chilled coupe or over fresh rock
codex.garnish: Citrus wheel, twist, or Angostura aromatic drops
codex.formula:
2.0 oz (60 ml) Base Spirit
0.75 oz (22.5 ml) Fresh Citrus Juice (Lemon or Lime)
0.75 oz (22.5 ml) Simple Syrup (1:1 or adjusted for 2:1)
codex.tip: Citrus acidity varies across seasons. Always straw-taste fresh juice daily; dial sugar back an eighth-ounce in midsummer when limes are sweeter, or bump it up when citrus is sharply astringent.
codex.lore: Derived from British Royal Navy rations where rum or gin was cut with lime juice and raw sugar to ward off scurvy, transforming medicinal necessity into the foundation of modern mixology.

codex.name: Amaro
codex.method: Neat, built over ice, or stirred as a cocktail modifier
codex.ice: Optional large rock with orange slice
codex.garnish: Orange peel or expressed lemon twist
codex.formula: Neutral grain spirit or grape distillate macerated with proprietary botanicals (gentian, rhubarb, cinchona, wormwood, cardamoms, citrus rinds) and aged in oak casks.
codex.tip: Lighter aperitivo styles (Aperol, Select) stimulate salivary flow before meals; darker, dense digestivo styles (Averna, Fernet, Cynar) rely on bitter alpine roots to ease digestion.
codex.lore: Born in medieval monasteries and apothecary shops across Italy as medicinal restoratives before flourishing in 19th-century piazza café culture.

codex.name: London Dry Gin
codex.method: Stirred, shaken, or built in highballs
codex.garnish: Lemon swath, olive, or lime wheel
codex.formula: Neutral spirit redistilled with natural botanicals dominated legally by Juniperus communis, coriander seed, angelica root, and citrus peels, with zero post-distillation sugar added.
codex.tip: London Dry is a production technique, not a geographic designation. It can be made anywhere worldwide provided all flavors are imparted purely through distillation without artificial additives.
codex.lore: The British Gin Craze of the early 1700s prompted Parliament to pass distillation acts that elevated crude 'bathtub' hooch into one of the cleanest, most sophisticated spirits in the world.

codex.name: Rye Whiskey
codex.formula: Distilled in the United States from a mashbill of at least 51% malted or unmalted rye grain, aged in virgin charred oak barrels at under 125 proof entry.
codex.tip: Rye whiskey possesses a sharp, peppery grain bite and herbaceous dryness that refuses to be overshadowed by sweet vermouth or herbal liqueurs in Manhattans and Sazeracs.
codex.lore: Rye was the dominant American whiskey prior to Prohibition, distilled by early Scottish, Irish, and German settlers across Pennsylvania, Maryland, and Virginia.

codex.name: Absinthe
codex.subline: The Green Fairy: Grande Wormwood, Anise & Fennel
codex.method: Slow French ice-water drip fountain or glass rinse
codex.formula: High-proof spirit redistilled with the 'holy trinity' of botanicals: Artemisia absinthium (grande wormwood), green anise seed, and Florence fennel.
codex.tip: A tiny atomizer mist (or a 1-barspoon rinse rolled around the glass interior) provides intense aromatics without overwhelming the delicate spirit balance of a cocktail.
codex.lore: Unfairly banned in 1912 due to moral panic and wine industry lobbying. Rigorous scientific testing in the 2000s proved vintage absinthes never contained hallucinogenic thujone levels, leading to worldwide legalization.

codex.name: Peychaud's Bitters
codex.subline: Creole Aromatic Bitters of New Orleans
codex.method: Dashed into cocktail tins and mixing glasses
codex.formula: Gentian-based aromatic tincture infused with anise seed, cherry bark, nutmeg, and clove, distinguished by its vibrant crimson hue.
codex.tip: Much lighter, more floral, and sweeter than clove-heavy Angostura. Indispensable for authentic New Orleans classics like the Sazerac and Vieux Carré.
codex.lore: Formulated in the 1830s by Antoine Amédée Peychaud, a Haitian apothecary who settled in New Orleans and dispensed medicinal toddies from his Royal Street pharmacy.

codex.name: Cocktail Specs
codex.formula: Standard documented liquid formulas specifying base spirits, modifiers, acids, sweeteners, dilution targets, and wash lines.
codex.tip: Always pour the cheapest ingredients first (citrus juices, simple syrups) before adding rare spirits. If you make a measuring mistake, you waste cents rather than dollars.
codex.lore: From 19th-century salon logbooks to modern digitized bar manuals, documented specs ensure a cocktail tastes identical regardless of which bartender is on shift.

codex.name: Shaking Technique
codex.method: Vigorous horizontal shaking with dense ice
codex.formula: Applied to any cocktail containing citrus, egg whites, cream, or fruit purées to emulsify liquids and incorporate thousands of microscopic air bubbles.
codex.tip: Shake horizontally with authority along the line of your shoulders. You are not simply cooling; you are creating a velvet foam cap and achieving 25% dilution in 10–12 seconds.
codex.lore: Patented in the mid-19th century, metal shaking tins replaced the risky practice of 'throwing' cocktails back and forth between two fragile glass tumblers.

codex.name: Stirring Technique
codex.method: Fluid push-pull glide around the interior wall
codex.ice: Dense, dry, solid ice blocks or cubes
codex.formula: Reserved exclusively for spirit-forward cocktails without juice or dairy (Martinis, Manhattans, Negronis) to chill without cloudiness or air bubbles.
codex.tip: Keep the back of the spoon flat against the interior glass wall. Drive the orbit using your fingertips, not your wrist or arm, keeping the ice mass moving smoothly as one unit.
codex.lore: Promoted by early London and New York private clubs to ensure spirit-forward cocktails remained gem-like, crystal clear, and luxuriously heavy on the tongue.

codex.name: Citrus Twist Expression
codex.glass: Coupe, Nick & Nora, or Rocks Glass
codex.method: Fold skin-side outward over the drink surface
codex.formula: Wide swath or strip of fresh citrus peel (lemon, orange, or grapefruit) cleanly cut with minimal bitter white pith.
codex.tip: Express the peel skin-side outward at a 45-degree angle 2 inches above the glass. The fine aromatic mist coats the surface tension so every sip is preceded by fresh aroma.
codex.lore: Standardized in late-19th-century hotel cocktail lounges to deliver volatile citrus oils without introducing citric acid into dry, spirit-forward drinks.

codex.name: Cocktail Ice Physics
codex.method: Directional freezing for pure crystal blocks
codex.ice: Large cubes, spheres, collins spears, crushed ice
codex.formula: Directional freezing freezes water from the top down, pushing dissolved air and minerals to the bottom to yield 100% transparent, dense thermal mass.
codex.tip: There is no chilling without dilution. Dense, dry, zero-void clear ice melts at a predictable, controlled rate, keeping a cocktail ice-cold without making it watery.
codex.lore: Boston 'Ice King' Frederic Tudor founded the global ice trade in the early 1800s, carving New England pond blocks and shipping them insulated in sawdust to tropical ports.

codex.name: Coupe Glass
codex.method: Pre-chilled with ice water or freezer staging
codex.formula: Broad, shallow bowl mounted on a slender stem designed for shaken or stirred cocktails served 'up' (without ice in the glass).
codex.tip: Always hold the vessel exclusively by the stem. Holding the bowl directly transfers hand heat to the chilled liquid, degrading the cocktail within minutes.
codex.lore: The urban legend that it was molded from Marie Antoinette's anatomy is historically false; the coupe was designed by English glassmakers in the 1660s for sparkling wine.

codex.name: Mise en Place
codex.method: Sanitation, staging, and muscle memory alignment
codex.ice: Freshly burned and refilled ice wells
codex.garnish: Garnish caddy cut fresh, squeeze bottles primed
codex.formula: The French culinary philosophy applied to the bar: everything in its deliberate, ergonomic place prior to welcoming the first customer ticket.
codex.tip: Speed is an outcome of economy of motion. When jiggers, tins, bottles, and fruit knives reside in identical muscle-memory positions, service flows effortlessly.
codex.lore: Perfected in legendary hotel bars like London's Savoy and the Paris Ritz, where master bartenders handled relentless rush tickets with serene calm.

codex.name: The Bar as Third Space
codex.method: Warm greeting, eye contact, thoughtful pacing
codex.formula: Physical wooden counter, speed rail, mirrored backbar, and stools creating a welcoming public social sanctuary.
codex.tip: A flawless drink cannot redeem cold service, but genuine hospitality and warmth can elevate an entire evening into an unforgettable memory.
codex.lore: Derived from the physical wooden barrier that separated patrons from spirits in 18th-century inns, the modern bar evolved into a democratic gathering space.

codex.name: The Staff Toast & Handshake
codex.glass: Shot Glass, Pony Glass, or Snifter
codex.formula: 1.0 oz neat measure (traditionally Fernet-Branca, Mezcal, Underberg, or Chartreuse) poured to welcome visiting industry peers.
codex.tip: Never toast in a way that interrupts guest focus or compromises clean professional service standards.
codex.lore: Fernet-Branca became celebrated as the global 'Bartender's Handshake' during the 2000s craft cocktail revival in San Francisco and New York.
